trade: Life skills class at the fire station's open day — learner and firefighter
header: Early-primary to upper-secondary life skills: noticing someone is hurt, keeping yourself safe, calling for help and giving clear information — never a clinical step.
name: First Aid Awareness: Call for Help
tagline: Stay safe, get an adult, call for help, say clearly where you are

badge.name: Help Called
badge.note: Danger checked, an adult fetched, help called and the location given clearly

hazards.label: Run straight to them across the road?
hazards.text: You ran straight towards the person without checking for danger. The first rule is to keep yourself safe, because a second person hurt means help has two people to reach; you look for traffic or other dangers first and get an adult.

hazards.label: Try to fix their arm yourself?
hazards.text: You tried to treat the injury yourself. This lesson is about calling for help, not treating; trained people will know what to do, and trying a treatment you have not been trained in can make things worse.

hazards.label: Hang up as soon as you have said what happened?
hazards.text: You hung up as soon as you had said what happened. The person on the phone may need to ask more questions or tell you what to do next; you stay on the line until they say you can go.

hazards.label: Say 'near the park' when asked where you are?
hazards.text: You gave a vague location. Help can only arrive where you tell it to; look for a street sign, a building name or a landmark and say it clearly, because a vague answer costs time.

find1.title: Notice what you need to know
find1.cue: Mark the three things to notice before you do anything else.
find1.why: Before acting, notice three things: whether there is any danger to you, whether the person is responding, and where exactly you are. Noticing these first keeps you safe and gives you what the person on the phone will ask for.
items: Keep yourself safe first. Do not go into danger.
You can tell the adult and the caller this. You do not need to do anything else.
Help needs to know exactly where you are.
decoy: a balloon from the open day
Not important right now. Notice what matters.

select1.title: Get a trusted adult straight away
select1.cue: Shout for, or run to, the nearest trusted adult.
select1.why: Getting an adult is almost always the fastest route to help, and it is the right first move for a young person. An adult can call, keep others back and take charge, so you are never left dealing with it alone.
select1.label: Get an adult

seq.title: Put the call in order
seq.cue: Where you are, what happened, how many people, then stay on the line.
seq.why: The person answering needs to know where to send help first, because that is what gets people moving. Then what happened and how many people are hurt help them send the right help; staying on the line lets them guide you until it arrives.
seq.oon: Out of order. Say where you are first, so help can start moving.

hold.title: Stay on the line
hold.cue: Hold the phone and listen until they say you can hang up.
hold.why: Staying on the line means the person answering can ask more questions and tell you what to do next, such as keeping the person still or waving at the arriving help. Hanging up early cuts that help off. If you are not sure what to say, the person answering will guide you with questions, so stay with them.
hold.brk: You hung up too early. Stay on the line until they tell you it is fine to go.
hold.label: Staying on the line

turn.title: Put the phone on speaker
turn.cue: Turn the phone to speaker so your hands are free and the adult can hear.
turn.why: Putting the phone on speaker lets the adult beside you hear the questions and answer too, and leaves your hands free to wave to arriving help. It is a small step that makes the call work better for everyone. Every detail you can give calmly is one less question the call-taker has to ask while help is on its way.
turn.label: Phone to speaker

gauge.title: Speak calmly and clearly
gauge.cue: Commit when your voice is calm and clear enough to be understood first time.
gauge.why: A calm, clear voice gets information across first time; a rushed or shouted one has to be repeated, which costs time. Taking a breath before speaking is the simplest way to be understood in an emergency. Saying where you are first, before anything else, means help can start moving even if the call is cut short.
gauge.label: Calm voice
gauge.miss: Outside the band. Too rushed and you have to repeat yourself. Take a breath and try again.

drag.title: Show help where to come
drag.cue: Drag the waving arm to the safe spot by the road where help will arrive.
drag.why: Showing arriving help exactly where to go saves time. Standing safely at the road edge, with an adult, and waving is a useful job a young person can do while trained people take over. Responders arriving at a busy place lose time finding the right spot, so a clear signal from a safe place gets them there sooner.
drag.label: Arm raised
drag.miss: Not in place yet. Take it all the way to at the road edge, safely.

select2.title: Say what you will not do
select2.cue: Say why you will not try to treat the injury yourself.
select2.why: Knowing what not to do is part of being helpful. Leaving treatment to trained people, and doing the things you can do well, staying safe, calling and guiding, is what actually helps the person most. Trying a treatment you have not been trained in can make things worse, and it takes an adult's attention away from calling for help.
select2.label: Not a clinical step

find2.title: Spot the problems in a classmate's plan
find2.cue: Look at the classmate's help plan and mark each problem.
find2.why: Help plans go wrong in predictable ways: running into danger, trying a treatment and giving a vague location. Spotting them in someone else's plan helps you remember the right order when it matters. The right order is always the same: stay safe, fetch an adult, call for help and say exactly where you are.
items: Check for danger first. Keep yourself safe.
Call, do not treat. Trained people will know what to do.
Look for a sign or landmark and say it clearly.

track.title: Stay steady until help arrives
track.cue: Hold yourself in band — calm and near the adult — until help arrives.
track.why: Waiting for help is hard, and it is tempting to do something, anything. Staying calm, close to the adult and ready to answer questions is the most useful thing to do until trained people take over. Moving about or crowding round only adds to the confusion that responders then have to sort out.
track.brk: You drifted from calm. Take a breath and stay beside the adult.
track.label: Steady until help arrives

record.title: Tell the adult what happened
record.cue: When help has arrived, tell the adult what you saw.
record.why: Afterwards, telling the adult clearly what you saw helps them and the responders. Keep it to what you saw, in order, the same way a clear report is written. Guesses about what caused it can wait; the responders need what you actually saw first.
record.label: What happened, told

share.title: Share the steps with the class
share.cue: Tell the class the steps: safe, adult, call, where.
share.why: Sharing the steps helps classmates remember them, and saying them out loud fixes them in your own memory. Short steps that everyone knows are exactly what helps in a real emergency. In a frightening moment people fall back on what they have practised, so the practice is the preparation.
share.label: Share with the class

checkin.title: Check in at the end of the lesson
checkin.cue: How did the lesson go? Which part was hardest?
checkin.why: A short check-in at the end tells the teacher who is confident and who needs another go, and gives each learner a moment to notice what they can now do. Nobody is marked here, and a teacher or trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk more.
checkin.label: End-of-lesson check-in

interrupts.label: Step back from the road
interrupts.alert: A car pulls up fast close to where you are standing near the road.
interrupts.cue: Step back onto the pavement with the adult; do not go into the road.
interrupts.why: Traffic is the danger you checked for at the start, and it can arrive at any moment. Stepping back to the pavement with the adult keeps you safe; you are no help to anyone if you are hurt too.
interrupts.miss: Nobody stepped back, and a classmate was nearly clipped by the car door. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.
interrupts.wrong: That does not keep you safe. Step back onto the pavement. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Back on the pavement with the adult. Safe first, then help.

interrupts.label: Give a clear location
interrupts.alert: The firefighter, playing the call handler, asks exactly where you are.
interrupts.cue: Give the street sign or landmark you noticed, clearly.
interrupts.why: A clear location is the single most useful thing a caller gives. The firefighter asks because that is the first thing a real call handler needs, and noticing a sign at the start makes it easy to answer.
interrupts.miss: You said 'near the park', and the practice responders went to the wrong side of it.
interrupts.wrong: That is too vague. Give the sign or landmark you noticed. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Clear location given. Help knows exactly where to come.

guide.after: Say where you are, what happened, and stay on the line.
guide.hazard: Stop. Keep yourself safe and get an adult first.

lateRecord: You tell the adult what happened once help has arrived — not yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the lesson.
